lead: the half-built thing on the bench has been there since a flat you no longer live in, and nothing in you has filed it as abandoned. the one under it and the one behind the door are waiting too.
sun: work goes cold and stays reachable. you take up a piece at four years' distance — yours or a stranger's — and carry on the line instead of starting again: the joint matched, the stitch picked up where it was dropped, the pencil marks left legible. people bring you their dropped work for this, and they bring it late, having spent years calling it a loss.
moon: nothing that leaves your hands gets counted, and here that runs into an assumption that nothing has left. a thing you gave away is still yours in the only sense you use the word: reachable, alterable, due another pass. so you take work back off people. the shelf they have lived with for six years goes home with you on a saturday and returns improved, unasked.
pull: nothing you have made has come to rest. every object you handed over is still out for one more pass, and the people living with them do not know they are drafts.
tension: a delivery date is a request to stop being able to reach something, and reaching is the whole apparatus, so the work goes out late or goes out while you are out of the room. everyone who has waited on you has learned to lift the thing off the bench themselves, and they do it with an apology in their face, having decided years ago that you cannot bear to let a thing be imperfect.
cost: a build somebody else walked away from goes to the end in its maker's hand, none of it in yours: the join invisible, nothing restarted, every decision of theirs honoured. people give you work for that which they would not give a professional. your thirty years exist as one continuous revision, and there is nothing anyone could be shown as a body of work, only the current state of everything.

lead: another man has worn your grandfather's watch for six years, at your suggestion. the drill is two flats away, and the money was called a loan by exactly one of the people at that table.
sun: lending costs you nothing, and that is the whole of why you are good at it. handing a thing over does not register as parting with it — the object is out, the way a person is out, and it comes back when it comes back. so you say yes at full speed, without the half-second other people take, and that half-second is where a lender decides whether this one returns it.
moon: what you own sits where it can be seen and no guard assembles around it. The Jewel does not arm, so the good things are in the front room and nobody has to ask twice. a visitor works out inside one evening that no second conversation is coming — no reminder, no cooling, no note kept — and what a person does with that information is entirely theirs.
pull: in your own account of it you have never been robbed. things go out, some of them do not come back, and the file stays marked out rather than taken.
tension: the ones who love you have started saying no on your behalf, to people they think are working you, and you have heard about none of it. generous is what they say to your face, warmly, with a decade of evidence for it. what they are watching is a house that empties in one direction, kept by an owner with no count of the direction, and the correction would mean telling you a friend of yours is a thief.
cost: somebody in trouble can have the thing you need on saturday, with no interrogation attached to the asking and no atmosphere on the return, and people raised on ledgers remember that years later. a theft has never happened to you. nothing gets to be taken, so nobody has ever been held to anything, and the two who did take are still on the list, still welcome, still asking.

lead: you go back to everybody. six households would say you are theirs; none could give an address for you, name the other five, or say what you do on an ordinary week.
sun: coming back is the one reliable fact about you, and it does the work a whole life usually does. you turn up at the same kitchen every autumn and the conversation picks up mid-sentence, at the temperature it was left at, with nothing owed for the gap. people date their years by your visits, because that is the whole of the record available to them.
moon: there is no location under any of it. a return usually reads against the place it came from, and yours arrives from nowhere anybody can picture, which is how The Veil turns each visit into a small private event rather than one stop on a circuit. you have never corrected the impression. correcting it would mean describing where you actually live.
pull: everyone you go back to believes they are the fixed point. you are the fixed point. under you there is only the going, and the visits are the only rooms you keep.
tension: two of them compared notes at a wedding, and what came out was not a life with gaps in it. neither had been lied to. each had built the missing part of you generously, out of what was absent, and had been living beside that version for years. there is nothing to confess at a moment like that, which is the difficulty — what people find out is that the part they filled in was their own work.
cost: you can walk back into a life you hold no standing in and be received at full temperature, with none of the maintenance everybody else has to do, which is why people who have lost everyone still have you. it runs one way. anyone who wanted to come to you would first have to be told where that is, and telling them is the one errand you have never run.

lead: nineteen years of the same argument, and it has never been over for longer than a season. you can make his case better than he can, and that is what keeps drawing you back into it.
sun: a truce is a gap in something still running. you leave the fight for four years and re-enter at the sentence it stopped in, without heat, the whole structure intact and the last thing he said still the last thing said. he has spent those four years understanding the matter to be over, because four years means over to everybody who is not you.
moon: The Claws will not let you hold one end. the grip that would close it has been available for years — you know which sentence would take him apart — and the other half of you carries his side in good faith, at full strength, better than his own people carry it. so the pressure goes on and comes off in the same motion, and nobody ever loses.
pull: you hold the sentence that would win it, and you have held his case for nineteen years with equal sincerity. the fight lives on that, and on nothing else.
tension: his brother stopped seating you two together nine years ago. you have been at that table twice since, both times by your doing. grudge gets said, and the temperature is wrong for it — there has not been a cold day in it. a dispute reopened warmly, by the one person in it with no ill will, is harder to refuse than an angry one. his people think you are working an angle; yours think you have gone soft.
cost: twenty years on, a wrong the family agreed to bury gets said out loud again and survives being said, because you arrive holding both accounts of it and nobody has to be wrong first. what nobody near you gets is a settled matter. every peace you are part of is re-agreed every few years, and only one person at that table finds the schedule normal.
